summary: Discusses extending TCP to provide transaction-oriented service, without altering TCP's virtual-circuit operation. It is a historic informational memo and was replaced by RFC 6247.

eli5.summary: TCP spends a while setting up each conversation. This paper asks how quick one-question, one-answer exchanges could be sped up.

questions: how does tcp accelerated open work
why does tcp have time-wait state
subtitle: Optimize TCP for fast request-response exchanges

tldr.problem: TCP's three-way handshake and TIME-WAIT state create overhead for short request-response interactions like DNS queries or remote procedure calls. Applications that need transaction-style service currently choose either slow TCP or unreliable UDP.
tldr.mechanism: T/TCP (TCP for Transactions) proposes bypassing the handshake with a cached per-host value (TAO), and shortening TIME-WAIT delays using monotonic sequence numbers to exclude old duplicate packets without a long timeout.
tldr.outcome: This is a historic informational document exploring the concepts. RFC 1644 provides the full specification. RFC 6247 later replaced this work, but the ideas were not widely deployed in standard TCP.

today: RFC 1379 is a historic informational document. It provides the conceptual foundation for T/TCP. The full specification appears in RFC 1644 (July 1994). T/TCP was never widely deployed in practice, and standard TCP implementations do not include these extensions. Later work in RFC 6247 revisited some of these ideas.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TCP provides a virtual-circuit service: connections are explicitly opened, data is transferred reliably over a full-duplex stream, and connections are explicitly closed. This model works well for long interactions like remote login or file transfer. However, many modern applications need a transaction service: a single request followed by a single response, with no long-lived connection.

Currently, transaction applications must choose between TCP's overhead (requiring extra handshake and close packets) or UDP's unreliability (no guarantee of delivery or duplicate protection). This memo explores extending TCP to efficiently support transactions while maintaining reliable, ordered delivery. The idea is to keep TCP's virtual-circuit service for applications that need it while allowing transactions to skip unnecessary overhead.
sections.eli5: TCP is like calling someone: you say hello, talk, say goodbye. Good for long conversations. For quick questions, you want to just ask and get an answer without all the greeting and farewell.

sections.title: Overhead in Standard TCP
sections.content:
In standard TCP, a simple request-response transaction requires at least 10 packets: three for the opening three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), two for sending the request and acknowledgment, two for the response and acknowledgment, and three for the full-duplex close sequence. The client observes a latency of 2*RTT + server processing time, where RTT is the round-trip time.

Additionally, after the connection closes, both ends must remain in TIME-WAIT state for approximately 240 seconds (or 2-4 minutes in practice). During this time, the same connection (defined by the source/destination IP addresses and ports) cannot be reopened. Since a 16-bit port field provides only about 64,000 available user ports, and each transaction must wait 240 seconds before reusing a port, the maximum transaction rate between two hosts is roughly 268 transactions per second—too slow for local area networks or high-speed applications.
sections.eli5: TCP takes at least 10 messages for a hello-question-answer-goodbye sequence. And then you have to wait 4 minutes before using the same phone number again.

sections.title: TCP Accelerated Open (TAO)
sections.content:
The core innovation is TCP Accelerated Open (TAO), a mechanism to bypass the three-way handshake. The idea is that if two hosts have communicated before, the server can trust a new SYN segment from the client without a handshake, based on a cached value from their previous transaction.

Each side maintains a per-host cache that remembers the highest M value (a monotonic counter) from the other side. When a new SYN arrives with an M value greater than the cached value, the server immediately accepts the request and can deliver the data to the application without waiting for the final ACK of the handshake. The client in turn echoes back an M value in the SYN-ACK to verify it is a legitimate reply to this transaction, not a leftover from a previous one.

If the TAO test fails (because there is no cached state, or the M value is not greater than the cache), the connection falls back to a normal three-way handshake, ensuring safety. This makes TAO an optional optimization that always succeeds eventually, even in hostile network conditions.
sections.eli5: If you have talked to a friend before, the next time they call, you skip saying hello—you just start talking. If something is wrong, you fall back to normal greetings.

sections.title: Shortening TIME-WAIT State
sections.content:
To support high transaction rates, TIME-WAIT delay must be reduced from 240 seconds to a much shorter period. TIME-WAIT serves two purposes: (1) ensuring the full-duplex close completes properly, and (2) allowing old duplicate packets from earlier connection instances to expire before they can cause errors. To shorten TIME-WAIT safely, a different mechanism must exclude duplicates.

The solution is a monotonic sequence X carried in every packet. When a segment arrives for a connection, it is rejected if its X value is less than the largest X value previously received. This protects against old duplicate packets without a long timeout. The TIME-WAIT delay can then be set to max(8*RTO, U), where RTO is the dynamically measured retransmission timeout. This typically reduces TIME-WAIT to a few seconds or less, allowing transaction rates up to millions of packets per second on fast networks.
sections.eli5: Instead of waiting 4 minutes, you assign each message a number and reject any message with an old number. That protects against mistakes without waiting.

sections.title: Choosing a Monotonic Sequence
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes several options for the monotonic sequence M/X: cached TCP timestamps, 32-bit TCP sequence numbers, 64-bit sequence numbers, and a dedicated connection count (CC). TCP timestamps (from RFC 1323) are too slow; they increment at most every millisecond, but transactions need to tick once per microsecond on fast networks. Standard 32-bit TCP sequence numbers can wrap, allowing old duplicates to be misinterpreted as new data.

64-bit TCP sequence numbers with very large initial sequence number increments could work, with wraparound taking millions of seconds. However, this requires changes to the TCP header format. The RFC recommends instead using a simple 32-bit global connection count (CC), incremented once per new connection. This is simple to implement (carried as a TCP option), and with an MSL of 2000 seconds, supports transaction rates up to one million per second. If timestamps are added to protect against wrap-around, even higher rates become possible.
sections.eli5: Every new connection gets a number. Old message numbers get rejected. The choice is: use fancy bits with 64-bit numbers, or just count connections. Connection counting is simpler.

sections.title: Connection State Changes
sections.content:
T/TCP introduces new connection states to the standard TCP state machine: SYN-SENT* and CLOSE-WAIT* and LAST-ACK* (marked with asterisks), which represent states where the TAO optimization has been used. In a transaction using TAO, the client sends a SYN with data and FIN to initiate and terminate in one segment. The server, if the TAO test succeeds, responds with SYN-ACK and data and FIN in the reply. The client acknowledges with a final ACK segment.

This three-packet exchange (down from ten in standard TCP) allows the entire transaction to complete in roughly RTT + server processing time, without the penalty of a four-minute TIME-WAIT on each side. The state machine transitions preserve the semantics of reliable delivery and proper connection closing.
sections.eli5: TCP's states now have special versions for fast transactions. Both sides quickly move to closed state, instead of waiting in TIME-WAIT.
